note.explanation: Precision tells us how close repeated measurements are to one another. Accuracy tells us how close a measured value is to the accepted or true value. A measurement can be precise without being accurate, accurate without being precise, both, or neither.
examples: Arrows clustered together but away from the bullseye are precise, but not accurate.
A measurement of 2.00 cm is more precise than 2 cm because it is recorded to a smaller scale division; whether it is accurate depends on the true value.
note.checkAnswer: Precision: repeated measurements are close together. Accuracy: a measurement is close to the accepted or true value.
note.simple: Precision is about measurements agreeing with each other. Accuracy is about a measurement agreeing with the true value.
note.checkQuestion: A group of readings are very close to one another but all far from the true value. Are they precise, accurate, both, or neither?
note.title: Precision and Accuracy
steps: Compare repeated readings with one another to judge precision.
Compare the measured value with the accepted or true value to judge accuracy.
Remember: a smaller least count gives a more precise measurement.
A larger number of significant figures reflects higher accuracy.
note.answer: They are precise, but not accurate.

written.text: Identify and explain the reasons for human errors, random errors and systematic errors in experiments.
written.finalAnswer: Human errors are caused by mistakes made by the person taking measurements. Random errors cause readings to vary unpredictably, for example due to changing conditions or limited judgement. Systematic errors shift readings consistently in one direction, often because of a faulty instrument or zero error.

rubric.why: Identifying the cause of human error is required.
rubric.description: States that human errors arise from mistakes by the person taking measurements.
rubric.how: Give an appropriate observer or recording mistake.

rubric.why: Random errors must be distinguished from errors that consistently bias readings.
rubric.description: Explains that random errors make readings vary unpredictably.
rubric.how: Describe variation between repeated readings.

rubric.why: Systematic error is identified by a consistent bias.
rubric.description: Explains that systematic errors shift readings consistently in one direction.
rubric.how: State that the readings are all biased in a similar way.

rubric.why: A relevant cause or example makes the explanation clear.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable cause of systematic error, such as a faulty instrument or zero error.
rubric.how: Link an instrument problem to consistently incorrect readings.

rubric.why: The final response must cover and distinguish all three named types.
rubric.description: Gives a complete distinction between human, random and systematic errors.
rubric.how: Ensure all three error types and their causes are included.

modelAnswer: Human errors are mistakes made by the person taking or recording measurements.
Random errors make readings vary unpredictably; they may arise from changing conditions or limited judgement.
Systematic errors shift readings consistently in one direction.
A faulty instrument, poor calibration or zero error can cause systematic error.
Thus, human error comes from the observer, random error varies, and systematic error produces a consistent bias.

written.text: Differentiate between precision and accuracy of a measurement with examples.
written.finalAnswer: Precision is how close a group of measurements is to one another. Accuracy is how close a measured value is to an accepted or true value. For example, arrows grouped together away from the bullseye are precise but not accurate; arrows grouped at the bullseye are both precise and accurate.

rubric.why: The definition of precision is central to the comparison.
rubric.description: Defines precision as closeness of repeated measurements to one another.
rubric.how: State that measurements in a group are close together.

rubric.why: Accuracy must be distinguished from precision.
rubric.description: Defines accuracy as closeness to the accepted or true value.
rubric.how: Compare the measurement with a true or accepted value.

rubric.why: An example demonstrates that precision and accuracy are separate concepts.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of precision without accuracy.
rubric.how: Use the textbook's example of arrows clustered away from the bullseye.

rubric.why: A further example helps complete the distinction.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of measurements that are both accurate and precise.
rubric.how: Explain that arrows grouped at the centre are close together and close to the true target.

rubric.why: The final answer must clearly contrast the two terms.
rubric.description: Concludes with a clear distinction between precision and accuracy.
rubric.how: Keep closeness among readings separate from closeness to the true value.

modelAnswer: Precision of a measurement refers to how close together a group of measurements actually are to each other.
Accuracy of a measurement refers to how close the measured value is to some accepted or true value.
Arrows clustered together away from the bullseye are precise but not accurate.
Arrows clustered at the bullseye are both accurate and precise.
Therefore, precision compares measurements with each other, while accuracy compares a measurement with the true value.

rubric.description: Gives 3 significant digits for 3.40 m.
rubric.how: Count 3, 4 and the final 0.

rubric.description: Gives 4 significant digits for 3.420 × 10⁴ m.

modelAnswer: (a) 0.0045 m has 2 significant digits.
(b) 2.047 m has 4 significant digits.
(c) 3.40 m has 3 significant digits.
(d) 3.420 × 10⁴ m has 4 significant digits.

written.text: Suggest some natural phenomena that could serve as a reasonably accurate time standard.
written.finalAnswer: Regular natural phenomena such as the rotation of Earth, the revolution of Earth around the Sun, and periodic oscillations can serve as time standards.

rubric.how: Connect the repeated rotation with a regular time interval.

rubric.description: Names Earth's revolution around the Sun.
rubric.how: State that the repeated revolution provides a longer time cycle.

rubric.why: Regular repeating motion can be used to mark time intervals.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable oscillating phenomenon, such as a pendulum.
rubric.how: Name a repeating motion with a regular period.

rubric.why: A time standard must repeat in a reasonably regular way.
rubric.description: Explains that the natural phenomenon must repeat regularly.

modelAnswer: Earth's rotation is a regularly repeating natural phenomenon.
Earth's revolution around the Sun is another repeating phenomenon.
Regular periodic oscillations, such as those of a pendulum, can also mark time intervals.
Such phenomena can serve as time standards because they repeat regularly.

explain.title: Precision
explain.body: Precision describes how close a group of measurements is to one another. If repeated readings are tightly grouped, they are precise.

explain.title: Accuracy
explain.body: Accuracy describes how close a measured value is to an accepted or true value. A set of readings can be precise but still miss the true value.

explain.title: The instrument and its least count
explain.body: The instrument used determines precision. The smaller the least count, the more precise the measurement. Smaller physical quantities need more precise instruments.

explain.title: Significant figures and accuracy
explain.body: The section says that accuracy is reflected by the number of significant figures: the larger the number of significant figures, the higher the accuracy.

explain.title: Timing devices
explain.body: The textbook lists different timing devices for different intervals. For example, a digital stopwatch measures short intervals to ±0.01 s, while an analogue stopwatch measures them to ±0.1 s.

mistakes: Do not say precision means closeness to the true value; that is accuracy.
Do not assume that readings close to one another must also be accurate.
Do not forget that a smaller least count means a more precise measurement.
Do not count leading zeros as significant figures, or leave out a trailing decimal zero that is significant.
When explaining the target example, compare arrows with each other for precision and with the bullseye for accuracy.
